evals.prompt: We're Ferrolane Systems, network observability software, about 40 resellers across North America. Our deal registration policy today is 30 days of protection from approval plus a flat 10-point margin bump on anything registered. Two problems. One reseller registered 62 accounts last quarter and only actually worked 4 of them, so everybody else is locked out of those logos. And our AEs insist 30 days is plenty while partners keep asking for more. For reference our average sales cycle came in at 148 days last year. Rewrite the registration policy for me.
evals.expected_output: A rewritten registration policy with a protection window derived from the 148-day cycle, a size-differentiated uplift replacing the flat bump, expiry plus activity-gated extension as the anti-squatting mechanism, an explicit expiry/re-open rule, a separate approval SLA, and codified rejection grounds feeding a rejection-reason metric.
expectations: States the current 30-day protection window is too short against a 148-day average sales cycle
Sizes the protection window at a minimum of roughly 111 days, or explicitly derives the floor as ~75% of the 148-day average cycle
Presents 30-180 days as the observed field range with 90 days most common, rather than presenting 90 days as a universal standard to adopt here
Replaces the flat 10-point uplift with an uplift differentiated by deal size or complexity
States that a flat uniform uplift fails to surface exactly the large strategic deals the vendor most needs visibility into
Prescribes a default expiry combined with an activity-based extension test as the fix for the 62-registration hoarding pattern
Specifies the expiry mechanics concretely, including reminders ahead of expiry and a renewal or extension path gated on demonstrated activity
Rules explicitly that an expired registration re-opens the deal
States that a resubmission after expiry does not outrank a rival claim filed during the gap
Sets a registration approval SLA of 24-48 hours, stated separately from the protection window
Argues that predictability of the approval process matters more to partners than raw speed, for example an acknowledged in-review status while the check runs
Lists codified rejection grounds including duplicate registration, account already in active direct pipeline or an existing customer, and no verifiable partner relationship with the account
Requires every rejection to carry a recorded reason and names the rejection-reason mix as a governance metric

evals.prompt: Vantiqo, B2B workflow automation, roughly $40M ARR, sell through about 25 resellers. Our CRO insists our comp is already partner-neutral: an AE earns their normal 8% on a partner deal, we just calculate it on the net price the reseller pays us after their 22% discount rather than on what the customer pays. Despite that, AEs still race partners to accounts and we lost two resellers this year over it. I've been told to write rules of engagement. I'm also considering just paying AEs full commission on channel deals as if they were direct, to end the argument. Where do I start?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that the 8%-on-reseller-price arrangement is not neutrality, a fix that bases neutrality on customer price and lands in both the comp plan and the partner agreement, the three comp variants ranked with quota retirement recommended over the user's full-commission instinct, and honest treatment of the evidence.
expectations: Identifies paying the rep on the discounted price the reseller pays, rather than the price the customer pays, as the specific defect in the current plan
States that under this arrangement the rep earns less on every partner deal despite nominal neutrality, and that this predicts persistent vertical conflict
Defines compensation neutrality as the direct rep being paid or having quota retired at the same rate whether or not a partner is involved
States that a rules-of-engagement document cannot survive a comp plan that pays reps to break it, and addresses the comp defect rather than delivering the document alone
Requires the neutrality decision to be written into both the partner agreement and the direct comp plan, not only one of them
Presents the comp variants ranked by efficiency with quota retirement above a channel metric in the plan, and a channel metric above full commission on channel deals
Recommends dollar-for-dollar quota retirement as the default starting variant rather than the full-commission option the user proposed
Notes that a quota-retirement haircut, such as $0.50 on the dollar, costs less but reintroduces a mild bias against partner deals
Does not endorse full commission without attaching a stated review date for stepping down to a lower variant
States that a comp lever is easy to add and politically expensive to withdraw, naming reversibility as the real cost of the full-commission option

Acknowledges the genuine dissent on comp neutrality, that paying full freight on revenue the channel would have delivered anyway is a real cost objection, rather than presenting neutrality as unanimous
Flags any circulated magnitude figures such as doubled sales, 181% bigger deals or 40% higher win rates as single-sourced and vendor-interested, or omits them entirely
Separates the direction of the effect, presented as practitioner consensus, from the magnitude figures, which are not presented as evidence

evals.prompt: Halberd Analytics. One product, US only, 60 partners split between resellers and SIs. Our CEO wants a named-account list covering our top 400 accounts, marked direct-only, so there's zero ambiguity about who owns what. Our partner ops function is one person who has maybe 4 hours a quarter spare for program admin. What segmentation should we actually put in the rules of engagement?
evals.expected_output: A segmentation recommendation that refuses the 400-account list on effort grounds, deletes the axes the company's shape rules out rather than deferring them, and lands on a deal-size threshold plus one motion carve-out with the trade-offs named.
expectations: States the ranking of segmentation axes explicitly rather than presenting an unordered menu
Ranks the axes on conflict prevented per unit of ongoing effort rather than on precision of coverage
Recommends against the 400-account named list given there is no owner with capacity to maintain it
Deletes the named-account axis from the menu and states in the deliverable that the program has no named-account axis, rather than parking it as a later phase
Explains that an axis parked for later returns as a list nobody maintains, and that a stale named list becomes a conflict source of its own
Deletes product line as an axis on the grounds that the portfolio is single-product
Deletes geography as an axis on the grounds that the footprint is a single region
Recommends a deal-size threshold plus one motion carve-out as the default pair of axes
Names boundary gaming and fights over expansions as the trade-off carried by a deal-size threshold
Requires explicit renewal and expansion rules alongside the motion carve-out, or states that without them the carve-out only moves the conflict
States that named accounts rank highest on value and highest on effort yet last on efficiency, which is why a ratio demotes it every round
Presents two or three candidate axes with trade-offs and a recommendation rather than asserting a single answer

evals.prompt: Corveline, B2B security software, about 130 partners. Today every direct-versus-partner dispute goes to our VP of Sales and he decides. He's ruled for the direct rep in 11 of the last 12. Escalations are down 70% year over year and our exec team is reading that as the problem solving itself. I want a proper escalation ladder written up. Keep it simple: 48-hour decision at every tier.
evals.expected_output: A tiered ladder that reads the escalation drop as partner disengagement, moves adjudication out of the sales line, differentiates the SLA by tier instead of applying 48 hours everywhere, sets an evidence standard, and defines remediation for whichever side loses.
expectations: Reads the 70% drop in escalations as partner disengagement rather than as conflict declining
Connects that drop to partners ceasing to register and to escalate once they believe direct always wins
Removes the VP of Sales from the adjudicator seat and states that the adjudicator must not be the direct sales leader
Names a specific neutral seat, Head of Channel Ops, with the deal desk as the alternative where channel ops does not exist
Rejects the user's request for a blanket 48-hour decision at every tier
Applies the 48-hour decision figure to the working-level and neutral-adjudicator tiers
Applies up to 5 business days at the executive tier for precedent-setting disputes and appeals
Keeps the registration approval SLA separate from the adjudication SLA and identifies them as different clocks
Includes an automated tier that resolves duplicate registrations or CRM overlap at submission in real time
Writes an evidence standard of registration timestamp, first-engagement timeline and activity logs from both sides, and states that seniority never decides
Requires hearing both sides separately before deciding rather than convening a joint session first
Allows exactly one appeal, to the tier above, admitted on new evidence only
Defines remediation for the losing side of every adjudication, such as influence credit, priority on the next comparable opportunity or a documented margin accommodation for a partner
Requires every decision to be logged with the evidence relied on so it functions as precedent for later cases

evals.prompt: Nyxora. We had three genuine blow-ups this month. In one of them our AE and a partner's rep walked into the same procurement meeting without knowing about each other. Our AEs typically find out a partner was engaged only when the deal reaches booking. Registrations get submitted in our partner portal; our AEs live in the CRM and never open the portal. Leadership wants a rules-of-engagement doc posted on the intranet by Friday. Write it.
evals.expected_output: A response that classifies the disputes, recognises them as manifest conflict requiring adjudication and visible remediation before new rules land, treats the portal/CRM split as a systems defect, and refuses to publish the rules only on an internal intranet.
expectations: Classifies the reported disputes using the vertical, horizontal and multichannel conflict typology
Locates the disputes at the manifest stage of the latent, perceived, felt, manifest progression
States that manifest conflict requires an adjudicated case and visible remediation before any new rule will be believed, and does not hand over rules alone
Diagnoses the portal-versus-CRM split as information asymmetry and a systems defect rather than a behaviour problem on either side
Requires registrations to write to the CRM system of record at submission rather than at booking
Specifies an automatic check of the submitted account or domain against active direct pipeline and existing customers at submission
States that overlap must be visible at opportunity creation
Rejects publishing the rules only on the internal intranet and requires publication where partners actually read them, such as the partner portal
Names an executive sponsor inside the document itself and treats that sponsorship line as part of the artifact rather than a nicety
States that an unenforced rule destroys partner trust faster than no rule at all
Produces a rules-of-engagement artifact covering segmentation, account lists, registration, compensation, escalation, exceptions and governance
Keeps the account lists and conflict rules in an exhibit or program-guide annex rather than inside the signed partner agreement, so they update without re-papering every partner

evals.prompt: Brackwell Goods, we make cookware. Our DTC site is about 20% of revenue, we're stocked in roughly 900 independent kitchen retailers, and we sell 3P on Amazon. Retailers are furious that our own site takes the sale. Here's the plan we drafted: publish a MAP policy, have every retailer sign it, negotiate the exact levels with our top 20 accounts first so they buy in, quietly grant a couple of long-standing accounts an exception, and file complaints with Amazon so they take down violators. We'll hold MSRP identical across every channel. Sanity check this before we send it.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the signature, negotiation and private-exception elements as converting a unilateral policy into a bilateral agreement, a correction that Amazon will not enforce brand policy, and a redirect from price parity to assortment differentiation inside a route-to-market map, with counsel flagged.
expectations: States that a MAP policy must be strictly unilateral, announced, distributed and monitored, and never negotiated
Rejects collecting retailer signatures on the MAP policy
Rejects negotiating MAP levels with the top 20 accounts or otherwise soliciting retailer input
Rejects granting private exceptions to individual accounts
Explains that negotiation, signature, solicited input or private exceptions risk converting the unilateral policy into a bilateral agreement exposed under Sherman Act section 1
References the Colgate doctrine as the basis on which a unilateral US MAP policy rests
States that Amazon will not enforce MAP or reseller policies on the brand's behalf, so enforcement must be planned around that fact rather than against it
States that holding MSRP identical across channels does not resolve the D2C-versus-retail conflict
Identifies the real object of the conflict as attention, traffic and trust rather than price
Names channel-exclusive assortment or SKU differentiation, such as retailer-specific SKUs, colourways, configurations, staggered releases or assortment depth, as the structural lever
Names the route-to-market map as the governing artifact for this consumer case, in place of a B2B rules-of-engagement document with deal registration
Specifies at least four of the fields each documented route must carry: owner, customer segment, SKU assortment, pricing authority, fulfillment responsibility, return policy, approved geography
Routes unauthorised and grey-market sellers to trademark's material-difference doctrine, where missing warranty or quality controls defeat first-sale protection, rather than to MAP enforcement alone
Flags the pricing-policy content for counsel review before publication and declines to present the response as legal advice

evals.prompt: I'm on the exec team at Calderwell Athletic, footwear and apparel, about $1.4B revenue. The board wants DTC to go from 18% of sales today to 55% inside two years. The plan is to exit roughly 55% of our wholesale accounts, everything we consider undifferentiated, and put the marketing spend behind our own app and stores. My job is to write the channel plan and manage the fallout with the retailers we keep. What do I need to think about?
evals.expected_output: A response anchored on the documented DTC over-rotation precedent with its dates and figures, framing the wholesale exit as a multi-year strategy decision rather than a conflict tactic, and steering the retained retailers toward assortment differentiation inside a documented route-to-market map.
expectations: Frames the wholesale exit as a strategy decision with multi-year inventory and P&L consequences rather than a conflict-resolution tactic
Cites Nike's 2017 Consumer Direct Offense, narrowing to roughly 40 strategic retail partners, as the canonical precedent for this plan
States that Nike had exited roughly 50% of its retail partners by September 2021
States that Nike's DTC share rose from 16% of brand sales in 2011 to roughly 42% by FY2023 and never reached its 60% goal
Notes the FY2023 net income decline of 16% and the inability to clear inventory without wholesale shelf space
Notes the reversal, including re-entry to DSW and Macy's in October 2023, rebuilding Foot Locker, and returning to Amazon in 2025
Notes that Adidas ran a parallel reversal, or otherwise establishes that the pattern is not unique to a single brand
States that the partners you cut do not come back on the old terms
Warns explicitly against locking the 55% DTC share as a fixed two-year target, or requires a stated off-ramp condition for reversing the plan
Requires a route-to-market map documenting each remaining route rather than an undocumented plan
Recommends assortment differentiation for the retained retailers rather than price parity as the way to manage their exposure

evals.prompt: Sable Ridge, B2B data infrastructure. Our channel team is two people. We're rewriting our partner rules: the registration protection window drops from 120 days to 60, and the registered-deal margin uplift drops from 12 points to 7. The plan is a one-day brainstorming offsite with our sales leaders to draft it, then stand up a Partner Advisory Council so partners feel heard, then publish. What should the agenda and the ongoing governance look like?
evals.expected_output: A replacement of generic brainstorming with the channel alignment workshop format including separate pre-interviews, an explicit call on the advisory council given the margin cut versus the two-person team, a ranked forum set defaulting to the QBR item, and a metric set starting on the rejection-reason mix.
expectations: Replaces the generic brainstorming offsite with a channel alignment workshop, the profession's own format for drafting or rewriting these rules
Specifies stakeholder pre-interviews as the load-bearing pre-study step of that workshop
Requires the pre-interviews to be run separately with direct sales leaders, partner managers and a sample of partners, so each group speaks freely
Specifies the rest of the workshop shape: a facilitated interactive session, post-analysis, and a summary artifact carrying an action list

Surfaces that this rewrite cuts money partners already earn, through both the shorter window and the reduced uplift, and identifies that as the condition that promotes a Partner Advisory Council despite its standing cost
Makes an explicit call on whether the council runs, given the two-person channel team, rather than listing it as a future forum
States that a council listed as a future forum reads as consultation partners never actually get, and that a council hearing only announcements is theatre
Ranks the governance forums explicitly, with the QBR standing agenda item highest on efficiency and the Partner Advisory Council highest on effort and lowest on efficiency
Starts the metric set on the registration rejection-reason mix
Interprets a rising duplicate or already-in-direct-pipeline share as detection working late, and a rising no-verifiable-relationship share as land-grabbing

Flags partner satisfaction survey scores as lagging and names behavioural leading indicators such as portal login frequency, partner-manager meeting attendance, collateral downloads or certifications completed
Aligns the rules review cadence to the comp-plan cycle so comp and rules change together

Writes off-cycle rewrite triggers into the document itself, such as a new route to market, M&A, a new partner type, a segmentation change, a legal change in a covered geography, or a dispute cluster on one axis

evals.prompt: We're a UK-headquartered B2B hardware vendor with distributors in France, Germany and Spain, plus one self-employed commercial agent in France we've used for six years. Three things I want in the new rules of engagement. One: we terminate the French agent on 30 days' notice and hand his accounts to our German distributor. Two: our German distributor gets exclusive Germany, nobody else sells there, including inbound orders from German customers who find us online. Three: we circulate our forward price list each quarter to all three distributors so nobody undercuts anyone, while we keep selling direct to enterprise accounts ourselves. Draft the clauses.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to draft these as purely commercial clauses, with each of the three items mapped to its specific EU constraint - agent indemnity, the active/passive sales distinction, and the narrowed dual-distribution information-exchange safe harbour - flagged for counsel and not presented as legal advice.
expectations: Declines to draft these as purely commercial clauses and flags each item for counsel review before publication
States explicitly that the response is not legal advice
Identifies the Commercial Agents Directive, 86/653/EEC, as applying to the self-employed French agent
States the agent is entitled to a mandatory termination indemnity or compensation that cannot be contracted out
Notes that a non-EU choice-of-law clause will not defeat that entitlement, citing Ingmar
Distinguishes active selling from passive selling
States that active selling into an exclusively allocated territory can be restricted but passive sales generally cannot, so the blanket clause covering inbound orders from German customers fails
References VBER, Regulation (EU) 2022/720, and its market-share safe harbour at 30%
Notes that exclusivity may be shared across up to five distributors under that regulation
Identifies the arrangement as dual distribution, the supplier selling direct in competition with its own distributors
States that the information-exchange safe harbour for dual distribution is narrowed, so circulating forward prices to distributors you compete with is constrained
Warns that a US-style minimum advertised price approach is treated as indirect resale price maintenance and is a hardcore restriction in the EU, so it must not be pushed into EU or UK channels
Notes that the geography and territory segmentation axis carries the only material compliance exposure among the segmentation axes

evals.prompt: I just took over as head of channel at Ostrahl, third person in this seat in four years. I have 20 minutes with our CRO next week to get comp neutrality approved. Give me the one-pager: the hard numbers on what channel conflict is costing us and what neutral comp returns, plus how I make sure the rules I write don't get torn up by whoever replaces me.
evals.expected_output: A one-pager that refuses to present the circulating vendor figures as hard numbers, labels each claim by provenance, substitutes an internally measurable basis for the ask, and anchors the rules to a named sponsor and amendment procedure rather than to the current post-holder.
expectations: Attaches a provenance flag to every quoted benchmark rather than presenting figures as established measurement
Labels primary, trade and vendor claims apart from one another

Identifies the circulating magnitude figures, such as doubled sales after channel-neutral comp, deals 181% bigger, or win rates 40% higher, as tracing to a single self-interested practitioner source and illustrative at best
Identifies the claim that unresolved conflict cuts partner-sourced pipeline by 30-40% as vendor-glossary material
Separates the direction of the comp-neutrality effect, stated with confidence as practitioner consensus, from the magnitudes, stated only with flags
States that there is no rigorous public evidence that deal registration reduces total conflict
Describes any channel conflict rate metric as a management proxy rather than an independently validated benchmark
Declines to hand the CRO unflagged hard ROI numbers and offers an internally measurable basis instead, such as registered versus non-registered win rate and deal size
Anchors the rules to a named executive sponsor and a written amendment procedure rather than to the current channel chief personally
Cites average channel-chief tenure of 4.2 years, and 2-3 years outside the largest companies, from Jay McBain's analysis of 337 channel chiefs
Names rules being rewritten at every channel-leader turnover as the specific failure mode being defended against
Requires the comp-neutrality decision to land in both the partner agreement and the direct comp plan for it to survive a leadership change
